candidates.text:
Let n be a positive integer. Call any three consecutive cells in one row or column a potential triple.

For n≥2 there are
T=2n(n-2)
potential triples. A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal potential triples: their starting positions can differ from the block's starting position by at most 2. Its three cells each belong to at most three vertical potential triples, so it meets at most nine vertical ones. Thus it meets at most 14 potential triples altogether. The same bound holds for a vertical block.

In a terminal configuration every potential triple has lost a stamp. Hence, if k blocks were removed,
14k≥2n(n-2),
so
k≥n²/7-2n/7.
Therefore b(n)≥n²/7-2n/7. For n=1 this inequality also holds because b(1)=0. Thus we may take c=2/7.

For the upper bound, first suppose m is a multiple of 5. In an m×m square remove horizontal blocks as follows, with q=0,…,m/5-1:

• in every odd-numbered row, remove columns 5q+1,5q+2,5q+3;
• in every even-numbered row, remove columns 5q+3,5q+4,5q+5.

These are disjoint three-stamp blocks, and their number is m(m/5)=m²/5. In each odd row the surviving cells in every five-column period have residues 4,5, while in each even row they have residues 1,2. Consequently no row contains three consecutive surviving cells. Moreover, no column has surviving cells in two consecutive rows, since consecutive rows have opposite parity. Hence no vertical triple survives either.

Now let n be arbitrary and put m=5⌊n/5⌋. Apply this construction to the upper-left m×m subsquare. Then greedily remove any remaining intact triple until none remains. Every additionally removed block contains a cell outside the m×m subsquare, since no intact triple lies wholly inside that subsquare after the initial construction. The additional blocks are disjoint, so they can be assigned distinct outside cells. Their number is therefore at most n²-m².

Thus a terminal configuration is obtained using at most
m²/5+n²-m²
= n²/5+(4/5)(n²-m²)
blocks. Since 0≤n-m≤4,
n²-m²=(n-m)(n+m)≤8n,
and hence
b(n)≤n²/5+(32/5)n.
Thus d=32/5 works. Together with c=2/7, this proves the stated inequalities for all positive n.

Let the cells be indexed by \((r,s)\), where \(1\le r,s\le n\). We may assume \(n\) is a positive integer.

For \(n\ge3\), there are
\[
2n(n-2)
\]
potential blocks of three consecutive cells: \(n(n-2)\) horizontal and the same number vertical. In a final configuration admitting no further block, every potential block contains a removed stamp.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal potential blocks: their starting columns can range over at most five values. Its three cells each lie in at most three vertical potential blocks, so it meets at most nine vertical potential blocks. Thus it meets at most fourteen potential blocks altogether. The same bound holds for a removed vertical block. Consequently,
\[
14b(n)\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For \(n=1,2\), the same inequality holds because \(b(n)=0\). Hence we may take \(c=2/7\).

For the upper bound, consider the infinite periodic marking in which \((r,s)\) is marked exactly when
\[
s+2r\pmod 5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
In each fixed row, the marked cells occur in disjoint runs of three consecutive cells, separated by two unmarked cells. From the \(n\times n\) sheet, tear out every such marked run that lies wholly within the sheet. These are disjoint horizontal three-stamp blocks. There are at most \(n/5+1\) of them in each row, hence at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n
\]
in total.

The infinite marking meets every horizontal triple, since no row has three consecutive unmarked cells. It also meets every vertical triple: for three consecutive rows in a fixed column, the residues \(s+2r\) are
\[
a,\ a+2,\ a+4\pmod5,
\]
which are distinct, and therefore cannot all belong to the two unmarked residues \(\{3,4\}\).

Let \(E\) consist of the first two and last two columns of the sheet; thus \(|E|\le4n\). Every marked cell whose column lies between \(3\) and \(n-2\) belongs to a marked run lying wholly inside the sheet. It follows that after the preceding removals, every surviving potential block intersects \(E\).

Now continue greedily, tearing out any available three-stamp block until none remains. Removing stamps cannot create a new block, so every additionally removed block intersects \(E\). Since these additional blocks are disjoint, each uses a distinct stamp of \(E\); hence there are at most \(4n\) of them. We have therefore produced a maximal configuration using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Thus \(b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n\), so one may take \(d=5\).

Therefore, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac17n^2- rac27n\le b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n.
\]

Take \(c=2/7\) and \(d=5\). Here \(n\) is a positive integer.

For the lower bound, suppose a terminal configuration was obtained by removing \(b(n)\) disjoint blocks. For \(n\ge2\), the original sheet contains
\[
2n(n-2)
\]
triples of three consecutive cells: \(n(n-2)\) horizontal and the same number vertical. Every such triple must meet a removed block.

A horizontal removed block meets at most five horizontal triples: their starting positions differ from that of the block by at most two. Its three cells each meet at most three vertical triples, in distinct columns, so it meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most fourteen potential triples. The same bound holds for a vertical block. Consequently
\[
14b(n)\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
whence
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For \(n=1\), this inequality is immediate because \(b(1)=0\).

For the upper bound, first consider the following period-five pattern on the infinite square grid. In every row \(i\), place horizontal blocks
\[
\{(i,i+5k),(i,i+5k+1),(i,i+5k+2)\},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
These blocks are pairwise disjoint. In row \(i\), the covered column residues are \(i,i+1,i+2\pmod5\), so the uncovered runs have length at most two. In a fixed column \(j\), a cell in row \(i\) is covered exactly when
\[
j-i\equiv0,1,2\pmod5.
\]
Thus the covered row residues are \(j,j-1,j-2\pmod5\), and again every three consecutive cells contain a covered cell. Hence every horizontal or vertical triple in the infinite grid meets this pattern.

On the \(n\times n\) sheet, remove all blocks from this pattern that lie wholly within the sheet. Each row contains at most \(n/5+1\) such blocks, so their number is at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n.
\]
Let \(S\) be the set of cells in the first two or last two columns; then \(|S|\le4n\). Any triple disjoint from \(S\) meets an infinite-pattern block, and because its point of intersection is at least two columns from either vertical edge, that entire horizontal block lies in the sheet and was removed. Therefore every triple still intact after the initial removals intersects \(S\).

Now greedily remove intact triples until none remain. Every additionally removed block intersects \(S\), and these blocks are disjoint, so there can be at most \(|S|\le4n\) of them. The resulting packing is terminal and uses at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n= rac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Hence
\[
b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n.
\]
Combining the two estimates proves the theorem with \(c=2/7\) and \(d=5\).

problem.theorem:
I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).
